t: Why Starship is a telco story
d: Launch cadence and next-generation satellites decide when phone-to-satellite coverage goes continuous. Why Starship matters to mobile operators.
x: Direct-to-cell lives or dies on one boring question: how fast can you put enough capable satellites over people's heads? That is why Starship belongs in a mobile briefing, not only a space one. What "continuous" actually means for a phone A low-orbit satellite stays in view for only a few minutes, and it is moving at roughly 7 km/s. [1] For a phone user, "coverage" means there is almost always another satellite ready to take over, with spare capacity in the beam. Sparse fleets create windows: texts and a few apps when the sky is clear, then nothing. Dense fleets start to feel like ordinary mobile fallback. Today's first-generation Starlink Direct to Cell service already runs on more than 650 dedicated satellites and reaches unmodified 4G phones outdoors. [2] That is enough for a useful safety net in partner markets, but not the always-on, city-grade experience carriers eventually want to sell. The next step is not a slogan. It is more satellites, with more radio power and more beams, flown often enough that gaps close. For the engineering behind the handset link — tiny phone antennas, Doppler correction, why services start with messaging — see how an ordinary phone talks to a satellite . Why bigger satellites help tiny phones The bottleneck is the handset. A phone has a small antenna and little uplink power, so the satellite has to do the heavy lifting with large phased arrays and smart beamforming. [1] Put simply: more aperture and more spectrum at the satellite end buy more capacity per user on the ground. That is the point of SpaceX's next-generation Starlink Mobile (V2) constellation. In early October 2026 the FCC authorised SpaceX to deploy up to 15,000 of these direct-to-device satellites in very low orbits between 326 and 335 km, with half to be in assigned orbits by 7 October 2032 and the full authorised fleet by 7 October 2035. [2][3][5] Light Reading reports SpaceX is targeting user speeds up to about 150 Mbit/s on V2, up from about 4 Mbit/s on the current generation; SpaceX itself says the V2 mobiles will deliver more than 100 times the bandwidth of today's Direct to Cell system. [2][4] Those figures are targets, not a promise that your phone will stream HD from a hillside tomorrow. But the direction of travel is clear: without a step-change in satellite capability, direct-to-cell stays a messaging and light-data add-on. Launch cadence is the real buildout plan Authorising 15,000 satellites is not the same as flying them. Light Reading notes SpaceX will lean on Starship to deliver the larger D2D satellites into orbit in volume. [2] SpaceX has said the same in its own updates: Starship's payload capacity is part of how the next Direct to Cell generation gets built, alongside exclusive spectrum and new phased arrays. [4] Starship reached orbit on its 28 September 2026 test flight; the vehicle is still proving reuse and cadence, not yet a routine airliner schedule. [2] For carriers and customers, that matters more than any launch-day livestream. Every quarter Starship slips is a quarter the denser, higher-capacity phone constellation stays on paper — which delays when "open sky" stops meaning "maybe later this hour". The FCC's 2032 / 2035 milestones set a regulatory clock. [2][3] Physics and manufacturing set a harder one: how many next-gen mobiles leave the factory, and how often a rocket big enough to carry them actually flies. What this does to carrier timelines Virgin Media O2 / T-Mobile and other Starlink partners. O2 Satellite is already live in the UK on Starlink Direct to Cell over O2's 1800 MHz spectrum; T-Mobile's T-Satellite has been commercial in the US since mid-2025. [6][7] Those services ride the first-generation fleet. The experience upgrade customers will notice — more apps, more reliable sessions, fewer "try again when a bird is overhead" moments — tracks the V2 buildout and Starship's ability to loft it. Spectrum deals and handset support still matter; without launch rate they are paperwork. VodafoneThree and AST SpaceMobile. The other UK horse is not waiting on Starship. It is waiting on AST's BlueBird fleet. Vodafone says UK beta testing needs about 45 AST satellites, now expected at the beginning of 2027 after earlier summer-2026 trial talk slipped. [8] AST's Block 2 BlueBirds are large (about 2,400 square feet of array) and only a handful fit per rocket — New Glenn is designed for up to eight per mission — so a failed or delayed launch immediately moves partner dates. [9][10] Same industry constraint, different rocket. See our UK D2D race and O2 Satellite pieces for how the two UK paths compare. In short: Starlink partners inherit SpaceX's launch cadence. AST partners inherit whoever is flying BlueBirds that month. Continuous phone coverage is a logistics problem dressed as a network one. What to watch next First operational batches of V2 Starlink Mobile satellites, and whether Starship is the vehicle that actually flies them at scale. [2][4] Whether Starship flight rate moves from test shots to a repeatable cadence — that, more than any single demo, gates when high-bandwidth direct-to-cell can feel continuous. AST's path to ~45 satellites for early-2027 partner betas, including New Glenn and Falcon manifests. [8][10] Our direct-to-cell tracker for which markets are live, trialling or still announced-only as those fleets fill in. Starship will keep making headlines for reasons that have nothing to do with your SIM. For Full Duplex, the telco story is narrower and more useful: launch cost and cadence decide when a normal phone stops treating the sky as a sometimes-network. t: Roaming vs travel eSIM vs satellite: what actually works abroad
d: Roaming, travel eSIMs and satellite-to-phone compared for UK travellers: what each does, what it costs and where it works.
x: Will my phone work when I land, and what will it cost? There are now three answers, and they do different jobs. Roaming keeps your own number and plan working abroad. A travel eSIM is a cheap data line you add for the trip. Satellite-to-phone is a safety net for places with no mast at all. It isn't a way round roaming charges. In eleven years inside mobile networks, most of the bill shocks I've seen came from people mixing these up. Here's what each does today. 1. Roaming: your own SIM, someone else's network When you roam, your phone uses a partner network abroad and your home operator bills you. You keep your number, so calls, texts and bank codes arrive as normal. Inside the EU, "roam like at home" is the law for EU customers: calls, texts and data are charged at domestic prices, subject to a fair use policy [1] . Since Brexit, UK customers no longer have that protection, so each UK operator sets its own terms. Here is what the big four publish today: O2 includes roaming in its Europe Zone on its tariffs at no extra cost. If your UK allowance is over 25GB, you can use up to 25GB in the zone, after which you need a data Bolt On [2] . EE charges £2.72 a day to use your allowances in its European zone on plans that started on or after 7 July 2021, and nothing extra on plans that started before that date [3] . Its EE plan terms set a 50GB fair use limit for data used in its Europe zone if your UK allowance is bigger than that, so check your own plan's terms [4] . Its current price guide lists a weekly EU pass at £16.50 and a 15-day pass at £30 [5] . Vodafone charges £2.75 a day in its Europe zone (Zone B) if your plan doesn't include European roaming. It also sells an 8-day pass for £16 and a 15-day pass for £21 [6] . A 25GB roaming fair use limit applies, and Ireland, the Isle of Man, Iceland and Norway (Zone A) are included [7] . Three charges £2.75 per 24 hours in its "Go Roam in Europe" destinations if you joined or upgraded on or after 18 December 2025, and £2 if you joined or upgraded between 1 October 2021 and 17 December 2025. Up to 12GB of your data allowance works in Europe. If you have a Spend Cap, it must be high enough to cover the charge or roaming won't work [8] . Further afield it jumps: Vodafone charges £8 a day in its Zones C and D [9] . Three charges £8 a day on newer plans [10] . EE's rest-of-world passes are £6 or £8 a day, depending on the zone [5] . Roaming is for trips, not living abroad. O2 treats more than 63 days of inclusive roaming in any four-month period as unfair use and can add surcharges after sending you a warning text [11] . Vodafone's equivalent is more than 62 days, or more use abroad than at home, over four months [7] . Two protections help: your provider must text you on arrival explaining charges and limits (unless you've opted out), and if you set a bill limit, it can only charge beyond it with your agreement [12] . Ofcom also warns that phones can roam by accident near borders, for example between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland [12] . Insider tip: your plan's start date matters as much as the network. Two people on the same operator can pay different roaming charges. 2. Travel eSIM: a second, data-only line for the trip An eSIM is a SIM built into the phone that you download instead of inserting. A travel eSIM is a prepaid data plan you add next to your normal line. You install it by scanning a QR code or through an app, and you need Wi-Fi to download it [13][14] . Three things decide whether it works for you: Your phone must support eSIM. On iPhone that means an iPhone XS, XS Max, XR or later [14] . MoneySavingExpert says most Pixels and iPhones have supported eSIM since around 2018, and Samsung flagships since 2020. You can check by dialling *#06#: if an EID number shows, the phone should be compatible [13] . Your phone must be unlocked. Apple says your iPhone can't be locked to a network if you want to use another provider abroad. Check under Settings > General > About for "No SIM Restrictions" [14] . UK operators have been banned from selling locked handsets since 17 December 2021 [15] . Older or second-hand phones are worth checking. You don't get your UK number on it. Worldwide travel eSIMs are generally prepaid data plans, and Apple separates them from local operators' plans, many of which do come with a local number [14] . Your UK number stays on your normal SIM. If you leave both lines on, the travel eSIM carries your data but "you might still incur roaming fees from your home eSIM", in Apple's words [14] . With the home line off, iMessage and FaceTime still work on your home number. On cost, Which? checked prices on 1 July 2026 for a 10-day trip to ten popular destinations outside the EU. The cheapest 5GB plan it found ranged from £5.99 to £13.63 depending on the country, and the cheapest unlimited plan from £15.15 to £27.00. Some prices were converted from dollars. Prices change and vary by destination and length of stay [16] . Ten days of roaming at £8 a day is £80. Where it falls down: bank codes still come to your UK number, so if you need them, leave the home line on and accept that its roaming rules apply. 3. Satellite-to-phone: a safety net with borders The newest and most misunderstood option. These services connect an ordinary phone to a satellite when there's no mobile signal. Today they carry texts and a few light apps, not general browsing, and each is licensed country by country. O2 Satellite (UK) is a £3-a-month Bolt On for pay monthly customers with a compatible phone. It covers texting, location sharing and apps such as WhatsApp, Messenger and maps. Standard voice calls, including emergency calls, aren't supported. O2 says it is "only available in the UK for now", and it isn't designed for use on planes or at sea [17] . t: Where phones are really talking to satellites: what Opensignal's new map shows
d: What Opensignal's D2D Satellite Map shows about where ordinary phones really connect to satellites, who leads, and why Europe is still quiet.
x: Satellite-to-phone launches get announced at a steady pace. Opensignal's D2D Satellite Map , launched on 12 October, is one of the first public attempts to show where phones are actually using them. [1][3] Each point is a place where a smartphone connected to a direct-to-device (D2D) satellite service at some point since 11 January 2026. [2] Opensignal says the map will be updated monthly. [2] The version online now uses data up to 20 September 2026. [1] Who leads Activity is concentrated in a few countries. According to Opensignal staff speaking to PCMag and Fierce Network, the map shows heavy use in the United States, with Australia, Canada, Chile, Japan, Peru and New Zealand also clearly lit, while most of the rest of the world is dark or nearly so. [4][5] Opensignal told PCMag and Fierce Network that more than 90% of the connections it detects are on Starlink. [4][5] These are largely the markets where Starlink's operator partners went live early: T-Mobile in the US, Rogers in Canada, Entel in Chile and Peru, KDDI in Japan, One NZ and Telstra. [14]–[19] That's a pattern, not proof. The map doesn't show which network each phone was on. Why Europe and Africa are quiet This part is my analysis, not Opensignal's. The simplest explanation is time. Europe's first commercial service, O2 Satellite, only went live on 26 February 2026, the day after Ofcom's rules letting handsets connect took effect. [7][9] Elsewhere in Europe, most of what exists is still trials. Orange España has a pilot in Valladolid, and Salt in Switzerland is waiting for Swiss approvals. [11][12] VodafoneThree's UK beta is now aimed at early 2027. [10] In Africa, Starlink phone launches are very recent. Airtel Uganda went live on 24 September, four days after the current data cut-off, so it can't show up yet. [13] Two other things hold the numbers down everywhere. First, Opensignal told PCMag the map only uses data from Android phones, collected through its own app and partner apps, because Apple doesn't give third-party apps enough access. [4] Second, D2D is a fallback. O2, for one, connects phones to the satellite only when there's no mobile signal, so a country with good coverage will show less use even if the service is live. [7] The scattered dots in countries with no service have an explanation too. Opensignal's FAQ says these are mostly edge cases, such as people roaming from a country that has a satellite plan. [2] What it means if you're on O2 Satellite The UK is on the map, but only lightly. ISPreview's look at the UK found O2 Satellite connections mostly in rural areas and along roads with patchy coverage, including a long stretch of the A34. [6] Three things are worth knowing: It isn't a coverage map. A dot means a phone connected there. A gap doesn't mean O2 Satellite won't work there. O2 says the service took its UK landmass coverage from 89% to 95%. [7] iPhone use isn't counted. O2 Satellite has worked on iPhone since 28 May, but none of that use appears on the map. [4][8] A connection isn't a message. Opensignal's Lian Carl told Fierce Network that a dot shows the phone reached a satellite, not that a text or any data was sent. [5] Opensignal says it plans to add how well these connections perform, not just where they happen. [3] That will be the version that matters most to O2 customers, because it will show whether a WhatsApp message actually gets through from a Welsh hillside. Until then, treat the map as a picture of where satellite fallback is being used, not a guide to where it works. Map and data: Opensignal . We link to the map rather than reproduce it. t: Goodbye GSM? The 2G and 3G switch-off around the world, explained
d: Who has switched off 2G and 3G, who's next, and why GSM is so hard to kill. A global guide to the switch-off, plus the satellite twist.
x: The networks that taught the world to text are being retired. Here's where things stand and why it matters for satellites. The global picture A July 2025 industry report filed with the ITU counts 131 operators in 65 countries and territories that have completed or planned 2G switch-offs, and 147 operators in 62 countries and territories that have completed, planned or are in progress with 3G switch-offs. [3] It notes the Orange group has mandated that 2G and 3G be switched off in Europe by 2030, though timing is likely to vary by country. [3] The UK EE and Vodafone have completed their 3G switch-offs, and Three has switched off 3G across most of the UK. O2 said it would follow in 2025. [1][2] All UK mobile network operators have told the Government they will switch off 2G by 2033 at the latest. [1] O2 said it would keep some 2G for several years, for example to carry emergency calls in remote areas without 4G, and would withdraw 2G and 3G access for inbound roamers from 1 October 2025. [2] USA and Australia According to Ofcom, all 3G networks in the USA have already been switched off. [1] In Australia, TPG Telecom switched off 3G in January 2024 and Telstra and Optus followed in late 2024. [4] Why GSM is so sticky 2G hangs on because of the long tail: alarms, meters, payment terminals, older phones and roaming visitors. That is why switch-offs come with migration programmes rather than a single flick of a switch. The satellite twist Today's direct-to-cell services connect to 4G phones. Kyivstar, for example, says its Starlink service works with 4G (LTE) smartphones. [5] So one future scenario is a world where legacy 2G coverage in remote areas gives way to 4G on the ground plus satellite in the gaps. That's our analysis, not an announced plan. t: How does an ordinary phone talk to a satellite? A plain-English guide
d: How an ordinary phone talks to a satellite: cell towers in orbit, why they fly low, the Doppler problem and why service starts with texts.
x: A cell tower in the sky In direct-to-cell systems, the satellite carries base-station functions (an LTE 'eNodeB'), so an unmodified smartphone connects using familiar protocols, much as it would to a distant mast. Traffic then goes down to ground stations or across inter-satellite links. [1] The satellite borrows the mobile operator's own spectrum, which is why your phone roams onto it automatically. [2] In the UK, for example, O2 Satellite uses O2's licensed 1800 MHz spectrum. [3] Why it has to be low A phone transmits with tiny power through a small antenna. To hear it, satellites fly in low Earth orbit and use large, high-gain phased-array antennas. [2] Long delays and random-access problems also restrict this design to low orbits. [1] The Doppler problem A low-orbit satellite moves at around 7.5 km per second at 600 km altitude, producing a Doppler shift of tens of kilohertz, and stays in view for only a few minutes. [4] In today's direct-to-cell systems the network does the correcting, pre-compensating downlink Doppler and post-compensating uplink, so existing phones work unchanged. [1] In the standardised 3GPP 5G 'NTN' approach, the phone helps out, using GNSS and satellite orbit data to pre-compensate itself. [5] Why it's texts first Bandwidth per beam is limited, so operators start with messaging. Kyivstar says it began with SMS 'due to the limited bandwidth of satellite channels', with voice and data to follow. [6] What you'll notice You'll usually need to be outdoors with a view of the sky, and services start with texts and selected apps. t: Where do MVNOs fit when phones connect to space?
d: Where MVNOs fit when phones connect to space: wholesale access, SMS platforms, pricing and the questions MVNOs should be asking.
x: Analysis from an MVNO insider. Between 2010 and 2016 I worked on the IVR and SMS workstream of Virgin Mobile's thin-to-thick MVNO programme (MTP), alongside EE, BT Wholesale and Huawei. Moving an MVNO from 'thin' (renting almost everything from the host network) to 'thick' (running more of its own core, messaging and customer platforms) teaches you one lesson: whoever controls the integration points controls the product. How satellite plugs in today Starlink describes its Direct to Cell service as integrating with operators 'similar to a standard roaming partner'. [1] The deals are struck with network operators who own the spectrum: VMO2 in the UK uses its own licensed spectrum transmitted from space. [2] That puts host networks in the driving seat. Who might get access Not every model runs through the big networks. Skylo reports around 40 partners, including MVNOs as well as operators, device makers and chipset suppliers. [3] In the US, T-Mobile, AT&T and Verizon plan a joint venture to pool spectrum and create a single platform for satellite operators to connect to. [4] Questions MVNOs should be asking Wholesale terms: will satellite fallback be included in host agreements, or sold as an add-on? Messaging and IVR: if a customer texts via satellite, do your SMS platform, short codes and service messages still work? On a thick MVNO, that's partly your stack. Emergency and support: how will your contact centre and IVR explain 'SAT' mode to a customer stuck on a hillside? Pricing: VMO2 charges £3 a month on Pay Monthly plans. [5] Can an MVNO match that price, or use satellite to stand out from rivals? My view: satellite fallback will become a standard feature, and T-Mobile's CEO has called it 'table stakes'. [6] MVNOs that don't secure it in their wholesale deals risk looking like they have less coverage. Sources Kyivstar launch release (includes Starlink description) Virgin Media O2 newsroom ABI Research: Top D2C satellite providers to watch in 2027 Light Reading: T-Mobile looks to new JV for D2D Ookla: O2 Satellite DCD, 24 July 2026

t: O2 Satellite: how the UK became Europe's first direct-to-cell market
d: How the UK became Europe's first direct-to-cell market: Ofcom's rules, O2's 1800 MHz spectrum, Starlink and the £3 O2 Satellite add-on.
x: On 26 February 2026, Virgin Media O2 switched on O2 Satellite , a satellite-to-mobile service powered by Starlink Direct to Cell. It made VMO2 the first operator in the UK and Europe to launch satellite-powered data services, aimed at 'not-spots' with no terrestrial coverage. [1] How the regulation came together Ofcom published a framework for authorising direct-to-device (D2D) services in mobile spectrum in December 2025. Ookla describes it as the earliest in any European country and notes that it broadly follows the FCC's Supplemental Coverage from Space model. [2] Ofcom approved VMO2's licence variation in February 2026. Licence-exemption regulations took effect on 25 February 2026, which allowed existing handsets to connect. [3] Spectrum and price The service runs over O2's licensed 1800 MHz spectrum, which is transmitted from Starlink's low-Earth-orbit satellites. At launch it cost £3 a month on Pay Monthly plans and came at no extra cost on 'Ultimate' tariffs. [2] Starlink says customers get data, voice and video through apps, plus messaging, in remote areas. [1] Why it matters This is the first time a normal phone on a UK network can fall back to a satellite without special hardware. [2] For operators, coverage stops being only about masts. Sources Virgin Media O2 newsroom, 26 Feb 2026 Ookla: Starlink-powered O2 Satellite puts the UK at the front of Europe's D2D race Ofcom announcement, Feb 2026

t: T-Satellite a year on: lifeline, not a replacement
d: T-Mobile's T-Satellite a year on: where it proved itself in disasters, where everyday use lags, and what the US says about demand.
x: T-Mobile launched T-Satellite with Starlink commercially in July 2025. It works on most modern smartphones and covers parts of the US with no cell towers. [1] T-Mobile says more than 150,000 people use it every day, and it now carries data for a set of satellite-ready apps including WhatsApp, Google Maps and AllTrails. [1] Where it proved itself: disasters T-Mobile says T-Satellite supported more than 250,000 users and 1.5 million messages during Winter Storm Fern, and delivered more than 100 Wireless Emergency Alerts. It is also expanding through reciprocal roaming in Canada and New Zealand. [2] Where it hasn't (yet): everyday traffic CEO Srini Gopalan has said satellite accounts for about 0.0002% of T-Mobile's network usage, and only 0.0003% in peak summer months. He calls it a 'complementary' service that will become 'table stakes'. [3] He also confirmed that the exclusivity deal with Starlink does not end in 2026. T-Mobile is working on a D2D joint venture with AT&T and Verizon. [3][4] The Full Duplex view Direct-to-cell is becoming a standard safety net, much as roaming once did. The bigger question is who controls the satellite layer, and that is what the carrier joint venture is about. Sources T-Mobile Newsroom: Reaching for the Stars T-Mobile Newsroom, 5 May 2026 DCD, 24 July 2026 Light Reading: T-Mobile looks to new JV for D2D

t: Starlink vs AST SpaceMobile: the UK's two-horse race for satellite-to-phone
d: Starlink vs AST SpaceMobile in the UK: Virgin Media O2 picked Starlink, VodafoneThree chose AST. How the satellite-to-phone race stands.
x: Two of the UK's big mobile groups have chosen different satellite partners. Virgin Media O2 + Starlink VMO2 launched O2 Satellite in February 2026 using Starlink Direct to Cell over 1800 MHz spectrum. [1][2] VodafoneThree + AST SpaceMobile UK beta testing is now planned for the beginning of 2027, once AST expects to have about 45 satellites in orbit — the number Vodafone says it needs to start. [5] That slips an earlier plan for customer trials in summer 2026 through Satellite Connect Europe, a Vodafone Group and AST SpaceMobile joint venture. The aim is still a service capable of data, voice and SMS. [4] Ofcom approved a licence variation in April 2026 allowing VodafoneThree to provide D2D services in its 900 MHz spectrum, and handset exemption regulations for that band took effect on 10 July 2026. [3] It builds on Vodafone's January 2025 video call made directly to an AST BlueBird satellite from rural Wales. [4] AST's ~45-satellite target for early 2027 is the same fleet milestone other partners are waiting on: Telus completed a first network integration test with AST in October 2026. [6] Why the band matters Lower frequencies such as 900 MHz generally travel further and get into buildings better than higher ones such as 1800 MHz, although capacity and satellite design matter too. O2 Satellite is already live on 1800 MHz; VodafoneThree's AST service on 900 MHz is still ahead of its UK beta. Worth watching how the two bands compare once both are serving customers. d: About Full Duplex: independent analysis of satellite-to-phone, direct-to-cell and mobile networks, written by an 11-year mobile network insider.
x: About Full Duplex Your phone is about to connect to space. Full Duplex explains what that means. Most coverage of satellites and phones comes from the outside looking in. Ours doesn't. Full Duplex is written by an 11-year mobile network insider who saw GPRS, EDGE, 3G, HSDPA and 4G arrive, and watched Nokia rise and fall up close. We know how networks really work, and we know hype when we see it. Now satellites are joining the network. Starlink, AST SpaceMobile and others are connecting ordinary phones straight from orbit, and that will change coverage, roaming, emergency services and how operators make money, from rural Wiltshire to the Philippines to sub-Saharan Africa. Full Duplex explains what's really happening in plain English, for anyone who works in telecoms, invests in it or just wants to know why their phone suddenly says "SAT". Written by Sam Beer

x: Where ordinary phones can connect to satellites today: live services, trials and announced direct-to-cell partnerships by country, with sources. United States T-Mobile Starlink live. SMS, data for selected apps, emergency texts. United States AT&T AST SpaceMobile trial. First handoff between a ground-based cellular network and a direct-to-device satellite network, 21 Oct 2026 near Granite Falls, Washington (Ericsson and Nokia kit); builds on earlier voice, text and video calls; moving towards beta, no commercial launch date. Canada Rogers Starlink live. Texting, text-to-911 and selected apps (WhatsApp, Google Maps, AccuWeather, X, CalTopo) since 9 Dec 2025, after a beta from July 2025; C$15/month for all Canadians; data and voice planned. Canada Telus AST SpaceMobile trial. First network integration test completed Oct 2026; targeting broadband data, voice and text; Telus expects service for customers within the next year; AST (20 Oct 2026) targets initial, intermittent Canada coverage before end-2026. United Kingdom Virgin Media O2 Starlink live. O2 Satellite: £3/month Bolt On (pay monthly, compatible phone) or included with Ultimate plans; data-only, so messaging and app-based data/voice/video work, but no native voice calls (including emergency calls). United Kingdom VodafoneThree AST SpaceMobile (via Satellite Connect Europe) trial. AST (20 Oct 2026) targets initial, intermittent UK coverage before end-2026; Vodafone's earlier guidance was beta testing in early 2027, once AST has about 45 satellites in orbit; targeting data, voice, SMS. New Zealand One NZ Starlink live. Satellite texting (since Dec 2024). Japan KDDI (au) Starlink live. Messaging; data for SAT-enabled apps. Japan SoftBank; NTT docomo Starlink live. Messaging. Australia Telstra Starlink live. Satellite texting (postpaid plans). Australia Optus Starlink announced. Signed July 2023; SMS was due late 2024. Delayed and re-evaluating its timeline; no launch date. Philippines Globe Starlink live. Commercial launch June 2026 (see source). Ukraine Kyivstar Starlink live. Launched 24 Nov 2025; messaging via apps and SMS, satellite-ready apps and location sharing on existing LTE phones; free to all ~15.5m Kyivstar 4G smartphone users. Chile Entel Starlink live. Messaging; data planned. Peru Entel Starlink live. SMS since Dec 2025; data for selected apps (WhatsApp, Google Maps, X, AccuWeather, AllTrails) since Apr 2026; postpaid plans. Switzerland Salt Starlink trial. Test SMS; launch subject to Swiss approvals. Spain Orange España (formerly MasOrange) Starlink trial. Technical pilot in Valladolid (announced Feb 2026); opened temporarily, free, during the July 2026 wildfires; no commercial service as of 7 Oct 2026. 41 countries Various MNOs, MVNOs and device partners Skylo live. Standards-based NTN services (see source). 60+ countries (contracts) 56 MNO and distribution contracts Elveo Mobile (Lynk + Omnispace) announced. Commercial service targeted early 2028. Bangladesh Banglalink (VEON) Starlink live. Launched 9 Oct 2026, first in South Asia; essential apps and location services beyond terrestrial coverage; needs a 4G phone and Banglalink SIM, accessed via the MyBL app. Kazakhstan Beeline Kazakhstan (VEON) Starlink live. Launched 28 Sep 2026, first in Central Asia; SMS and basic internet/messaging apps (up to 2 Mbit/s) beyond terrestrial coverage; LTE Android phones for now; free promo until 30 Nov 2026. Uganda Airtel Uganda Starlink live. Launched 24 Sep 2026; SMS and selected light-data apps (incl. WhatsApp) on compatible smartphones beyond Airtel's terrestrial network. Brazil Vivo (Telefônica Brasil) Starlink live. Vivo Satélite live since 26 Oct 2026 on eligible plans with compatible 4G/5G phones: WhatsApp (messages and voice calls), SMS, MMS, RCS, iMessage, Google Messages, Google Maps, Apple Maps and the Vivo app; free promotional period for business customers until 26 Jan 2027. France Orange Skylo live. Message Satellite: SMS and location sharing when there's no mobile or Wi-Fi coverage, since 11 Dec 2025 (consumers); Orange 5G/5G+ plans on Google Pixel 9 (not 9a), 10 and 11 only; no voice or data; free until 31 Dec 2026 for sign-ups up to 18 Nov 2026, paid after; Orange Business option €5 excl. VAT/month.
